title: SAP Business Network for Logistics 2611 – What's New?
author: CorinnaKramer
text:
The November 2026 release of SAP Business Network for Logistics delivers a compelling set of improvements for shippers and carriers alike. The headline is e-invoicing: carriers can now generate and legalize compliant e-invoices for Germany directly within SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration — no external tools, no manual file exchange. Alongside that, this release opens a long-awaited connectivity channel with AS2. 
 Whether you are a shipper navigating compliance requirements, a carrier looking for simpler connectivity and a richer network presence, or an operations team working with EDI integrations — there is something directly relevant for you in this cycle. 

 Cross SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace 
 Faster error recovery in the 'Manage Integration Log' app 
 The number of error codes eligible for automatic reprocessing in the 'Manage Integration Log' app has been increased from 4 to 24. This is a meaningful operational improvement: common, self-recoverable errors — such as temporary connectivity issues or timing conflicts — no longer require manual intervention. 
 Key benefit: Less manual effort for integration support and faster recovery from transient errors in the integration log for both SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace. 
 New secure industry-standard channel for EDI: AS2 connection type 
 Carriers and data contributors can now select AS2 as a connection type when configuring their system integration in the 'System Connections' app — alongside the existing REST/API and SOAP options. 
 With AS2 now supported, carriers can connect using the protocol they already have in place, with no need to build or procure a new API capability. The connection is secure, encrypted, and industry-standard, meeting the requirements of shippers who mandate a trusted, auditable EDI channel. 
 Key benefit: Easier and faster carrier onboarding for carriers running AS2 infrastructure, reduced connectivity barriers, and a broader range of integration options to match carrier capabilities. 
 For more information, see: 
 Configure AS2 Connections in System Connections (Carrier) 
 Specifying the Authentication Details and Base URLs for Your System’s Endpoints (Carrier) or Specifying the Authentication Details and Base URLs for Your System’s Endpoints (Data Contributor) 
 Connectivity 

 SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration 
 E-invoicing for outbound scenarios — now available for Germany 
 This is the headline feature of the 2611 release. SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration now supports outbound e-invoicing flows, with Germany (XRechnung) as the initial scope. 

 What this means in practice: Shippers and carriers in Germany — or with German billing addresses — are facing increasing pressure to move away from PDF or email invoices and adopt fully compliant, structured e-invoices. Until now, this required either an external legalization service or a separate process outside the network. With this release, invoice legalization and the generation of a compliant XRechnung document happen directly within SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration, integrated with the existing settlement and dispute process. No separate system, no manual file handling. 
 How it works: 
 1: The shipper activates e-invoicing for their carriers via a toggle in the 'General Settings' app under a new 'E-Invoicing' tab. Before activation, the system displays a warning about the additional legal information carriers must provide — shippers should confirm carriers are ready before switching on the toggle. 

 2. Once enabled, shippers can configure tax-application settings per ordering party — with options for header-level taxes, item-level taxes (required for XRechnung compliance in many scenarios), or carrier choice. 

 3. When a carrier creates an invoice via the Web UI or API, the invoice is automatically submitted for legalization. A compliant XRechnung document is returned and forwarded to the shipper's transportation management system 
 4. If a discrepancy triggers a dispute, the dispute and correction cycle operates on the already-legalized document throughout — ensuring compliance is maintained end to end. 

 Current scope and known restrictions: 
 Initial release covers Germany (XRechnung). Additional countries and clearance models are on the roadmap. 
 Outbound flow only: carriers creating invoices within the SAP system. The inbound flow — where carriers submit an already-legalized invoice generated outside SAP — is planned but has no committed delivery date. 
 Carriers retrieve the generated e-invoice via download from the Web UI. EDI support for e-invoicing is currently out of scope. 
 Key benefit: Shippers and carriers can meet German e-invoicing compliance requirements without leaving SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration, reusing their existing settlement workflow and avoiding the cost and complexity of a separate legalization service. 
 A dedicated feature detail deck and a carrier how-to video — covering exactly what carriers need to prepare and how to submit an e-invoice — are available! 
 Improved carrier experience: EDI support extended 
 Two updates to Message Implementation Guidelines (MIGs) improve the data that can be transmitted via EDI for freight tendering: 
 EDI 204 (freight tendering): The last stop in an EDI 204 message now absorbs all remaining NTE (Note/Special/Instruction) segments with no cap. Previously, NTE data beyond a fixed limit was dropped, meaning special handling instructions, access notes, or operational comments could be silently lost in transit. This fix ensures all instructions flow through cleanly, regardless of volume. 
 IFTMIN D96A (EDIFACT counterpart to EDI 204): You can now add FTX+AAQ free text entries inside the GID (goods item details) loop for SSCC, gross weight, net weight, and gross volume. This brings IFTMIN D96A on par with EDI 204 for item-level detail on order instructions. 
 Key benefit: More complete and reliable data transmission for carriers integrating via EDI, with fewer silent data losses on complex freight orders with multiple notes or item-level details. 

 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 
 The 2611 release marks a significant step forward for compliance-driven use cases — particularly with the arrival of e-invoicing for Germany — while continuing to build out the connectivity and carrier profile foundations that make SAP Business Network for Logistics more valuable with every release. 
 As always, we recommend reviewing the What's New page on SAP Help Portal for the complete list of changes and technical details relevant to your setup. 
 Have questions or want to discuss the new features with other users? Join the conversation in the SAP Business Network for Logistics community

title: Relembre a palestra: SAP Agents - The Autonomous Enterprise #SITCWB2026
author: AdrianoCWB
text:
No dia 7 de novembro, no Auditório Gregor Mendel da PUCPR, Christian Geronasso, Business Development, apresentou no SAP Inside Track Curitiba 2026 a palestra "SAP Agents - The Autonomous Enterprise". 
 Sobre a palestra 
 Christian partiu das tendências de Amy Webb para 2025: IA agêntica, biologia generativa, o fim da privacidade individual, a dominância da computação espacial e a insegurança da informação. 
 Depois mostrou os gargalos estratégicos das empresas: execução vale mais que adoção (a era da experimentação acabou), 72% dos CEOs se veem como principais decisores da estratégia de IA, e o valor vem do redesenho dos fluxos de ponta a ponta, com foco em "compressão de velocidade". 
 A geopolítica da infraestrutura de IA 
 O argumento central: energia e hardware, e não os modelos de software, são as restrições reais da IA, e a escassez de energia é o gargalo físico mais imediato. Segundo as anotações da palestra, há 10.395 data centers no mundo, 37% deles nos Estados Unidos, e a disponibilidade fica em torno de 3%. A cadeia de chips depende de poucas empresas, como a TSMC (Taiwan) e a ASML (Holanda), o que cria uma dependência externa mesmo para quem vende o hardware. 
 Riscos que ele destacou 
 Cibercrime em escala industrial, com IA. 
 Economia da identidade: provar que você é humano passa a ser uma das transações mais valiosas. 
 "Silicon Wall": segregação de tecnologia e de dados entre países. 
 Fragilidade da cadeia de suprimentos de IA, por causa de geopolítica e dependência externa. 
 Requalificação em "decision literacy": ensinar os times quando delegar à IA. 
 E o ecossistema SAP? 
 Na parte final, a palestra mostrou como a IA chega ao dia a dia SAP: o Generative AI Hub no SAP BTP, com escolha entre vários modelos, orquestração, filtro de conteúdo e mascaramento de dados, a Joule e mais de 2.700 habilidades de IA embarcadas nos processos. Fechou com a jornada do especialista na era da IA. 
 Para levar 
 IA não é só software: depende de energia, chips e política. 
 Quem decide a estratégia de IA é a liderança, e o ganho está em redesenhar o trabalho, não só em adotar a ferramenta. 
 Preparar as pessoas para decidir quando delegar à IA é tão importante quanto o treinamento técnico. 
 Sobre o palestrante 
 Christian Geronasso, Business Development.

title: Configuring Bin Capacity Check Based on Volume of Product Master and Bin
author: Navinchaubey
text:
Configuring Bin Capacity Check Based on Product and Storage Bin Volume in SAP EWM 
 Introduction – Why Does Bin Capacity Matter in a Warehouse? 
 One of the common challenges in warehouse operations is ensuring that products are stored without exceeding the physical capacity of a storage bin. 
 Consider a distribution warehouse that handles products of different sizes and volumes. Some products occupy very little space, while others consume significantly more storage space. During putaway, warehouse operators may select a bin based on availability, but an available bin does not necessarily mean that it has sufficient capacity to accommodate the incoming quantity. 
 For example, imagine a storage bin with a maximum capacity of 10 GAL. The bin already contains products occupying 8 GAL, and a new putaway task proposes another 5 GAL of product volume. 
 Although the bin has sufficient physical availability in terms of stock placement, it cannot accommodate the additional 300 liters without exceeding its defined capacity. 
 Without an appropriate capacity check, the system could potentially direct products to bins that do not have sufficient space, resulting in operational challenges such as overcrowding, inefficient space utilization, and additional warehouse movements. 
 This is where SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM) volume-based capacity checking becomes useful. 
 During one of the warehouse solution design considerations, an important question is how to make putaway decisions based not just on whether a bin is available, but also on whether it has sufficient physical capacity for the incoming products. 
 SAP EWM provides different capacity-checking options, including checks based on volume and weight. In this scenario, we focus on volume-based capacity checking, where EWM considers the product volume maintained in the product master and compares it against the capacity defined for the storage bin. 
 The objective is to make the putaway process more intelligent by allowing EWM to validate the available bin capacity before confirming the destination. 
 Rather than relying entirely on warehouse operators to make these decisions, we can leverage standard EWM functionality to perform these validations during putaway. 
 Business Scenario – What are we trying to achieve? 
 Let's consider a distribution warehouse where multiple products are stored in the same storage area. Each product has a different volume, and each storage bin has a predefined maximum volume capacity. 
 The warehouse wants to ensure that the putaway process considers the actual space occupied by the products rather than simply checking whether a bin is available. 
 During the solution design, there are different ways to approach this requirement: 
 Manual bin selection: Warehouse operators identify suitable bins based on their knowledge of available space. However, this approach depends heavily on operator experience and may result in inconsistent space utilization. 
 Fixed bin assignment: Products are assigned to predefined storage bins. This can work for products with predictable storage requirements, but it may not provide sufficient flexibility when product quantities or volumes change. 
 Weight-based capacity checking: EWM validates whether the total weight in a bin exceeds its defined weight capacity. This is useful when the primary storage limitation is the load-bearing capacity of the bin or rack. 
 Volume-based capacity checking: EWM calculates the volume occupied by existing and incoming products and validates whether the destination bin can accommodate the additional quantity. 
 For this particular scenario, volume-based capacity checking is the appropriate approach because the primary business concern is the physical storage space occupied by products. 
 Expected System Behavior 
 The business expects SAP EWM to perform the following validations during putaway: 
 Read the product volume maintained in the product master. 
 Determine the volume occupied by the existing stock in the destination storage bin. 
 Calculate the volume required for the incoming putaway quantity. 
 Compare the total required volume against the maximum capacity maintained for the storage bin. 
 Allow putaway when sufficient capacity is available. 
 Reject the proposed destination when the available capacity is insufficient. 
 Continue searching for another suitable storage bin based on the configured putaway strategy. 
 Example: 
 Assume the following master data and stock situation: 

 Parameter 
 Value 

 Product 
 182 

 Product volume 
 0.25 GAL 

 Incoming quantity 
 20 EA 

 Maximum bin volume 
 10 GAL 

 Existing stock volume 
 8 GAL 

 Calculation: 
 Incoming volume = 20 × 0.25 = 5 GAL 
 Available bin capacity = 10 - 8 = 2 GAL 
 Since the incoming volume of 5 GAL exceeds the available capacity of 2 GAL, EWM should not propose this bin for the complete quantity. 
 In this situation, EWM should not allow the incoming stock to be placed in the same bin because the total volume would exceed its maximum capacity by 100 liters. 
 If another suitable storage bin is available, the putaway strategy should direct the stock to that alternative bin. 
 This ensures that storage capacity is considered as part of the putaway decision rather than leaving the responsibility entirely to warehouse operators. 
 In the following sections, we will walk through the required master data and SAP EWM configuration to achieve this functionality using standard volume-based capacity checking. 
 Configuration and Master Data Prerequisites 
 Before testing the functionality, we need to configure the storage type and maintain the required product and storage bin data. 
 Step 1: Define the Storage Type Capacity Check 
 SPRO Navigation: 
 SCM Extended Warehouse Management → Extended Warehouse Management → Master Data → Define Storage Type 
 For this scenario, configure the storage type to perform the required volume capacity check at Product level. 
 The capacity-check setting determines which capacity validation EWM performs during storage bin determination. 

 Step 2: Maintain Product Volume in the Product Master 
 Transaction: /SCWM/MAT1 in decentralized or MM02 for embedded EWM system. 
 Execute transaction /SCWM/MAT1 or MM02 
 Enter the product number. 
 Select the relevant warehouse or Plant in MM02. 
 Navigate to the Units of Measure section. 
 Maintain the product volume and volume unit for the relevant unit of measure. 
 Example:

 If the product is maintained in multiple units of measure, ensure that the volume information and conversion relationships are correctly maintained for the relevant units. 
 This information is used by EWM to calculate the volume occupied by the product quantity. 
 /SCWM/MAT1

 Step 3: Maintain Maximum Volume in the Storage Bin 
 Transaction: /SCWM/LS01 or /SCWM/LS02 
 Execute transaction /SCWM/LS01 to create a storage bin, or /SCWM/LS02 to change an existing bin. 
 Enter the warehouse number. 
 Enter the storage type. 
 Enter the storage bin. 
 Navigate to the storage bin capacity-related fields. 
 Maintain the maximum allowed volume and corresponding volume unit. 
 Example:

 Ensure that the maximum bin volume is maintained correctly. 
 EWM uses the product volume and the available bin capacity to validate whether the proposed putaway quantity can fit into the destination bin. 
 Step 4: Configure Putaway Strategy 
 The capacity check is part of the putaway bin determination process. Therefore, the storage type must also have an appropriate putaway strategy. 
 For example, consider the following strategies: 
 Addition to Existing Stock 
 For the Addition to Existing Stock strategy, EWM first attempts to find a bin containing the same product, subject to the configured stock placement restrictions and capacity check. 
 If sufficient capacity is unavailable, EWM can continue searching for another suitable bin according to the configured strategy. 
 End-to-End Putaway Execution 
 Once configuration and master data are maintained, we can test the functionality through an inbound delivery. 
 Execution steps: 
 Create an inbound delivery with reference to a purchase order. 
 Receive the inbound delivery in EWM. 
 Create a warehouse task for putaway. 
 EWM determines the destination storage type based on the storage type search sequence. 
 EWM search for a suitable storage bin based on the configured putaway strategy. 
 EWM checks the available volume in the proposed storage bin. 
 The system validates the existing stock volume and the incoming product volume. 
 If sufficient capacity is available, the warehouse task can be created with the proposed destination bin. 
 If sufficient capacity is unavailable, EWM searches for another suitable destination bin. 
 Testing Scenario – Capacity Validation Across Multiple Bins 
 Let's consider three storage bins with different existing stock volumes. 
 Incoming delivery quantity = 20 LB. 
 Product volume = 0.250 GAL per LB. 
 Incoming volume = 5 GAL.

 Existing Volume 
 Available Volume

 10 GAL 
 8 GAL 
 2 GAL 

 RAWM101 
 10 GAL 
 0 GAL 
 10 GAL 
 Expected capacity-check result: 
 RAWM100: Not suitable because only 2 GAL is available. 
 RAWM101: Suitable because 10 GAL is available. 
 EWM will propose bin RAWM101, provided it is selected by the configured putaway strategy and satisfies the other storage restrictions. 

 Note: If we do not have any space in any of the bins and if warehouse operator tries to force the bin RAWM1000, system will give an error. 

 Important Implementation Considerations 
 During implementation, the following points should be validated: 
 Product volume must be maintained correctly in the warehouse product master. 
 The volume unit of measure must be compatible with the storage bin volume unit. 
 Unit-of-measure conversions must be maintained for alternative units. 
 Maximum volume must be maintained for the storage bins. 
 The storage type must have the appropriate capacity-check setting. 
 Existing stock volume must be considered during capacity validation. 
 Mixed storage and addition-to-stock settings must be considered. 
 The putaway strategy determines how EWM searches for alternative bins. 
 Test both full quantity putaway and scenarios where the incoming quantity exceeds the available capacity. 
 Conclusion 
 SAP EWM provides standard functionality to validate storage bin capacity based on product volume and the maximum volume maintained for the storage bin. 
 By implementing this functionality, organizations can prevent overfilling storage bins, improve warehouse space utilization, and reduce manual intervention during putaway. 
 For warehouses handling products with different dimensions and volumes, this is a useful standard capability to incorporate into the EWM solution design. 
 The key to a successful implementation is maintaining accurate product volume, storage bin capacity, and the appropriate storage type capacity-check settings.

title: Migration from Fiori Groups to Pages
author: Vaishnavi_R_Kamble
text:
Migration from Fiori Groups to Pages: what I found when I tried “Create Launchpad Pages from Groups” on S/4HANA 2025 
 If you are moving from Fiori groups to spaces and pages, the app “Create Launchpad Pages from Groups” can save you time. 
 I tried it on our S/4HANA 2025 on-premise system (SAP_UI 816) after upgrading from 1709. 
 In this post I cover what the app does, what to check if the tile is missing, and a lesson about launchpad modes that caused us support tickets. 

 1. What the app does 
 It converts each selected group into a section of a new page, with the same title and content. You select groups with the Group ID filter and can merge several into one page. You then fill in Page ID, title, description and transport, and choose Create Page. The page is only a starting point. Review it in Manage Launchpad Pages and add it to a space in Manage Launchpad Spaces. SAP itself says groups and spaces can’t be converted fully automatically. 
 /UI2/FLP_GTP is the transaction. 
 /sap/bc/webdynpro/ui2/ is the service path. 
 SAP Fiori Apps Reference Library - SAP Public ALM 
 SAP Fiori Apps Reference Library 
 2. What to check if the app is not visible 
 I couldn’t see the tile in my admin space, and the T-code redirected me to the home page. 
 This is the order I checked things in: 
 SE93: display /UI2/FLP_GTP to confirm the transaction exists in your system and see what it starts. 
 SICF: use the service path /sap/bc/webdynpro/ui2/, find the service FDM_GTP (“GTP Migration Tool”), and use Test Service. If the app opens, the app itself is fine, and the problem is in the launchpad configuration. 
 Launchpad Content Manager (Client Specific): on the Tiles/Target Mappings tab, search “Create Launchpad Pages from Groups”. The tile originates in the technical catalog SAP_TC_FLP_COMMON, and SAP_BASIS_BC_UI_FLD references it. 
 Show Usage in Roles: this lists which roles contain the catalog. Check whether your own role is among them. 
 Apps Reference Library: check the app’s Business Catalogs section. 
 Catalog access only makes the app available to you. SAP distinguishes between business catalogs granting access and the space and page deciding whether the app shows on the launchpad. Create a reference to the tile in your own custom business catalog and include that catalog in a custom role. Then place the tile on a page in a space assigned to that role. 
 3. A lesson from our 1709 to 2025 upgrade 
 SAP’s guidance for migrating from groups to spaces and pages is to enable spaces first without making them the default, using SPACES_ENABLE_USER = true. 
 SPACES_ENABLE_USER controls whether users can switch to “Use Spaces” in User Actions > Settings. 

 In our case, after the upgrade, the spaces and pages option was left to the user. 
 Several users who were familiar with the old screen unticked it. They were then back on the old-style launchpad, where some apps didn’t work for them, and we started receiving support tickets. To avoid this, we set the default in the system so that nobody could opt out of the new launchpad. SPACES_ENABLE_USER is now false, and every user lands directly on the latest launchpad. 
 Takeaway: letting users choose is helpful while you are testing and training, but after go-live, decide on one launchpad mode for everyone. 

 Conclusion 
 Converting groups to pages is a starting point, not a finished migration. Always review the generated pages in Manage Launchpad Pages and assign them to spaces. 
 If the app is missing, check the transaction, the SICF service, the catalog and role assignment, and the space and page placement in that order. 
 And after go-live, pick one launchpad mode for all users instead of leaving it as a user choice. 
 I’d be glad to hear how others handled this, so please share your experience in the comments.

title: Smarter Selling Starts Here: How AI Powers the Lead-to-Opportunity Stage in SAP Sales Cloud Version
author: Parisa_Mahdavi
text:
Sales professionals spend a significant portion of their time on activities that AI can now handle better and faster — deciding which leads to call first, researching accounts before a meeting, gauging whether a deal is at risk, and preparing talking points tailored to a specific customer. SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 embeds AI capabilities directly into the sales workflow to address exactly these challenges, helping sellers prioritize more precisely, understand customers more deeply, and walk into conversations better prepared. 
 This post walks through each AI capability available in the Lead-to-Opportunity stage and explains what it does, how it works, and where it delivers value. 
 Base AI vs. Premium AI: Understanding the Two Tiers 
 SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 distinguishes between two categories of AI capability: 
 Base AI — delivered out-of-the-box with the standard license at no additional cost. Includes Lead & Opportunity Scoring, Sentiment Analysis, and Relationship Intelligence. 
 Premium AI — requires AI Units for activation. Includes Account Synopsis and Lead Booster. 
 This distinction matters when planning adoption: Base AI capabilities are available immediately, while Premium AI requires license planning but unlocks generative AI features that go significantly further in depth. 
 Lead & Opportunity Scoring — Prioritize the Pipeline With Predictive Intelligence 
 Not all leads deserve equal attention. The challenge has always been knowing which ones to focus on. Lead & Opportunity Scoring answers that question using machine learning. 
 How Lead Intelligence Works 
 The Lead Intelligence model is trained on your organization's historical lead data — specifically leads that were converted into opportunities and leads that were declined. From these patterns, the system builds a customer-specific predictive model and applies it to score all open leads. 
 Scores range from 0 to 99 and are grouped into three color-coded bands: 
 0–50 : Less likely to convert 
 51–75 : Likely to convert 
 76–99 : Very likely to convert 
 For accurate scoring, the model requires a minimum of 1,000 converted and 1,000 declined leads , at least 12 months of lead lifecycle data , and sufficient data volume in any custom fields added to the scoring scenario. 
 Key Factors — Transparency Behind the Score 
 When a sales representative opens a scored lead, the Insight section displays up to six factors that most influenced the score, split across two types: 
 Dynamic Key Factors : Adaptive factors whose influence changes over time, such as Activity Count, Qualification Level, and Last Interaction — categorized as highly influencing (green) or minimally influencing (red). 
 Static Key Factors : Non-changing attributes such as Account Industry, Lead Source, and Lead Priority. 
 This transparency is important: sellers can see not just the score, but why a lead received that score and what signals are driving the prediction. 
 How Deal Intelligence Works 
 Deal Intelligence applies the same principle to opportunities. The model is trained on historical won and lost opportunities and assigns a win probability to each open deal — enabling sales representatives to prioritize their pipeline based on data-driven probabilities rather than intuition alone. 
 Scores are dynamic , refreshing daily around midnight in the data center's timezone using the latest customer data, interactions, and KPIs. Administrators configure both models under System Settings → AI Configuration → Narrow AI, with a Readiness Report verifying whether sufficient historical data exists before model training begins. 
 Sentiment & Relationship Intelligence — Reading the Room, Mapping the Network 
 Knowing a lead's score tells you where to focus. Understanding the emotional tone of your customer communications and the strength of your relationships tells you how to engage. 
 Sentiment Analysis 
 SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 uses Natural Language Processing (NLP) to analyze text from emails and surveys and determine whether the language is positive or negative — and how intense that sentiment is. 
 For sellers working through the Lead-to-Opportunity stage, this provides an automated emotional pulse of customer communications. Negative sentiment shifts can flag at-risk leads before they go cold. Positive sentiment can signal readiness to progress — prompting the right follow-up at the right time. 
 Relationship Intelligence and Hugrank 
 Relationship Intelligence automatically builds a smart network map of your organization's professional relationships. At the center of this is Hugrank — a quantitative measure of relationship strength scored from 0 to 100 , calculated based on approximately one year of communication history including email recency, frequency, reply rates, and calendar events. 
 Hugrank is grouped into three bands: 
 70–100 : Strong, active relationship 
 40–69 : Average, needs attention 
 0–39 : Poor engagement, at risk 
 Hugrank scores are accessible from the Relationship Intelligence facets within account and contact records and from the "My Network" workcenter in SAP Sales Cloud and SAP Service Cloud Version 2. 
 The business value in the Lead-to-Opportunity stage is direct: sellers can identify warm connections within an account, leverage internal colleagues who already have strong relationships with key stakeholders, and navigate deal cycles more effectively by understanding who knows who and how strong those relationships are. 
 Account Synopsis — Walk Into Every Conversation Prepared 
 First impressions in sales conversations are hard to recover from. Walking into a meeting without knowledge of an account's business challenges, competitive landscape, or strategic priorities is a missed opportunity — and manual research takes time that most sellers do not have. 
 Account Synopsis is a generative AI feature that produces a comprehensive, AI-generated summary of a customer account across multiple configurable dimensions, including: 
 Business Overview 
 Competitive Landscape 
 Business Challenges 
 Business Strategies 
 The synopsis is generated dynamically , reflecting the current market situation rather than relying solely on manually entered CRM data. Administrators activate it under System Settings → Generative AI Settings, choosing which sections to display for their organization. 
 In the Lead-to-Opportunity stage, Account Synopsis delivers value by: 
 Enabling sales representatives to walk into first conversations with deep account knowledge, addressing specific pain points and demonstrating industry awareness 
 Accelerating account planning by providing structured intelligence without manual research 
 Supporting lead qualification by helping sales reps assess whether the account's needs and strategies align with the products being offered 
 Facilitating more personalized engagement that builds trust and increases conversion probability 
 Account Synopsis is a Premium AI capability requiring AI Units. 
 Lead Booster — From Knowing Which Lead to Knowing How to Approach It 
 Lead & Opportunity Scoring tells you which leads to prioritize. Lead Booster tells you how to approach them. 
 Lead Booster is a generative AI feature that provides customized, AI-generated selling intelligence for each individual lead. It generates tailored content across configurable themes, including: 
 Company Understanding 
 Industry Needs 
 Pain Points 
 Strategic Alignment 
 Product Benefits 
 Scalability, Customization, and Competitive Advantage 
 The content is generated based on the account context, the products associated with the lead record, and market intelligence — meaning the guidance is specific to that lead, not generic talking points. 
 Lead Scoring vs. Lead Booster — Two Capabilities, One Workflow 
 Aspect Lead Score Lead Booster 
 AI Type Predictive ML (supervised learning) Generative AI (LLM-based) 
 Purpose Prioritize which leads to pursue Guide on how to approach each lead 
 Output Numeric score (0–99) + key factors Structured text with selling themes 
 Training data Previously converted/declined leads Account context + market intelligence 
 License Base AI (included) Premium AI (requires AI Units) 
 Update frequency Daily batch scoring On-demand generation 
 The two capabilities are designed to work together: scoring identifies the opportunity, Lead Booster equips the seller to act on it. 
 In the Lead-to-Opportunity stage, Lead Booster delivers business value by: 
 Reducing time spent on lead research and conversation preparation by up to 90% 
 Helping new or less experienced sales representatives perform at the level of seasoned account managers by providing ready-to-use selling guidance 
 Increasing conversion rates directly by enabling more relevant and consultative initial conversations 
 Lead Booster is a Premium AI capability requiring AI Units. Products must be entered in the lead record for product-specific guidance to be generated. The feature is currently available on iOS mobile devices. 
 A Connected AI Layer Across the Sales Workflow 
 These capabilities are not isolated features — they form a connected layer of intelligence across the Lead-to-Opportunity stage: 
 Lead & Opportunity Scoring tells sellers where to focus their pipeline 
 Sentiment Analysis surfaces the emotional tone of ongoing communications 
 Relationship Intelligence maps the strength of stakeholder connections 
 Account Synopsis provides deep, structured account knowledge before the first conversation 
 Lead Booster delivers lead-specific selling guidance at the moment of engagement 
 Together, they address the core challenge of the Lead-to-Opportunity stage: helping sales professionals identify the right prospects, understand them deeply, and engage with the kind of relevance and preparation that turns leads into opportunities. 
 Lead & Opportunity Scoring and Sentiment & Relationship Intelligence are Base AI capabilities included in the standard SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 license. Account Synopsis and Lead Booster are Premium AI capabilities requiring AI Units for activation.

title: How AI Is Reshaping Marketing in SAP Engagement Cloud
author: Parisa_Mahdavi
text:
Marketing has always involved a degree of guesswork — which subject line will get opened, which product will resonate, which contact is ready to buy. AI is steadily replacing that guesswork with precision. SAP Engagement Cloud (SAP Emarsys) and SAP Customer Data Platform embed AI capabilities directly into the platforms where marketers already work — not as separate tools to switch between, but as integrated intelligence woven into campaign creation, delivery, reporting, and audience targeting. 
 Here is a practical walkthrough of what those capabilities are and what they actually do. 
 SAP Engagement Cloud: AI Built Into Every Stage of the Campaign 
 Better First Impressions, Faster 
 The subject line is the single most important variable in email marketing. It determines whether an email gets opened or ignored — and writing good ones at scale is harder than it sounds. 
 The Subject Line Generator , built directly into the Visual Content Editor (VCE), solves this through a two-phase process. In the first phase, it scans the email body, extracts keywords, identifies the purpose and tone, and captures brand signals. In the second phase, it feeds that analysis to a large language model (LLM) to produce a configured number of subject line variants — ready to rate, use, or refine. 
 The result: marketers get multiple high-quality options in seconds instead of drafting variations manually. In a contact-to-lead context, a stronger subject line drives higher open rates, which means more contacts engage with content and move closer to conversion. 
 Preheader Generator — The Second Line of the First Impression 
 If the subject line gets the email opened, the preheader seals the deal. The short preview text that appears after the subject line in most email clients is frequently underused — written as an afterthought or left as a default placeholder. 
 The Preheader Generator treats the preheader as a strategic element. It analyzes both the subject line and the email content together and generates preheader variants that complement and extend the subject line's message — not just repeat it. 
 An Autogenerate Preheader checkbox takes this further: when enabled, the preheader is generated automatically without any additional manual steps, streamlining campaign creation for high-volume teams. 
 AI-Assisted Report Builder — Analytics Without the Technical Bottleneck 
 Understanding campaign performance has traditionally required either technical query skills or dependence on a small number of people who have them. Neither is efficient at scale. 
 The AI-Assisted Report Builder changes the dynamic by allowing marketers to ask plain-language questions and receive structured campaign reports in return — no technical skills required. Questions like: 
 "What was the revenue from SMS campaigns last month?" 
 "What are the monthly year-to-date and year-over-year comparisons for Open Rate, Click Rate, and Conversion Rate for my batch campaigns?" 
 The AI translates the question into a reporting schema — metrics, date range, grouping, filters, sorting — and generates a structured report with table visualizations. If a question cannot be fully answered, the tool surfaces alternative questions based on the original query. 
 For marketing teams, this means faster decisions and broader access to analytics across the organization, without creating a bottleneck on technical resources. 
 Send Time Optimization — Right Message, Right Person, Right Moment 
 Even the most compelling email fails if it arrives at the wrong time. Sending a campaign to your entire audience at a single fixed time ignores a simple reality: different people check their email at different times. 
 Send Time Optimization (STO) addresses this by analyzing each recipient's historical email engagement behavior and delivering the next email at the individually optimal time — not a single blast, but a staggered, personalized delivery across the audience. 
 The algorithm balances two behaviors: 
 Exploitation : Using existing historical data to send at times already known to perform well for a specific contact. 
 Exploration : When little historical data exists, experimenting with different send times to discover better engagement windows. 
 The more campaigns you run, the smarter STO becomes. For scheduled campaigns, sends are distributed from 00:00 through to 22:00 on the launch day. For manually launched campaigns, sends are staggered over 24 hours from when calculations complete. 
 The compounding effect matters: every additional campaign adds more behavioral data, making each subsequent send more precisely timed than the last. 
 SAP Engagement Cloud Predict — Real-Time Personalization at Scale 
 Personalization is one of the most frequently cited marketing priorities and one of the least frequently delivered at scale. Predict is SAP Engagement Cloud's machine learning-powered recommendation engine — and it is built specifically to close that gap. 
 Predict analyzes behavioral data collected from your web shop: page views, add-to-cart events, checkouts, and search queries. It uses that data to deliver personalized product recommendations across email, web, and mobile in real time. 
 A key architectural strength is the Unified Profile. Predict recognizes users across multiple channels and devices and combines their browsing behavior into a single profile. Anonymous profiles are matched with identified contacts as soon as an identification event occurs — such as clicking a tracked email link — ensuring maximum coverage across all touchpoints. 
 Revenue attribution is tracked through a dedicated dashboard: web recommendation revenue is attributed when a customer clicks and purchases in the same session; email recommendation revenue is attributed when a contact purchases anything within seven days of clicking through. A/B testing is available across all delivery channels to validate the impact of Predict recommendations against existing approaches. 
 SAP Customer Data Platform: Predictive Intelligence for Smarter Targeting 
 While SAP Engagement Cloud focuses on how you communicate with contacts, SAP Customer Data Platform focuses on who to target, when , and why — applying machine learning directly to unified customer data to generate forward-looking predictions about behavior. 
 Predictive Indicators — Acting on What Customers Are Likely to Do Next 
 Not all contacts are equal. Predictive Indicators help you act on that reality by generating machine learning-powered scores from existing customer profile, group, and activity data. 
 Four core model types are available — each applicable to both individual Profiles and Groups: 
 Model What It Predicts 
 Propensity to Buy Which contacts are most likely to make a purchase 
 Churn Which contacts are at risk of disengaging 
 Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) Expected profit margin over a defined period 
 True Customer Lifetime Value (TCLV) CLV refined by subtracting product returns — more accurate for high-return industries 
 The practical implication is significant: rather than treating every contact the same, your team can prioritize high-propensity leads, re-engage at-risk contacts before they go cold, and allocate marketing investment where it will generate the greatest return. 
 AI Workbench — A Centralized Intelligence Hub 
 The AI Workbench is the advanced analytics and model management environment within SAP Customer Data Platform. It is designed for business analysts and data-science-oriented users who need more than standard dashboards — bringing predictive models, visual insights, and performance monitoring into a single workspace. 
 The workbench is organized around three pillars: 
 Dashboards bring multiple insights together into a single monitoring view — for example, combining Customer Lifetime Value Profiles, Churn Probability Distribution, and Churn Risk Over Time into one consolidated screen. 
 Insights provide ready-to-use visualizations to help teams interpret predictive results without creating custom reports: 
 Churn Insights : Show churn risk by segment and the distribution of churn probabilities 
 CLV Insights : Show average CLV, profile distribution, and CLV trends over time 
 All insights are parameterized by solution, predictive indicator, and run ID, and support time periods from days (up to 365) through to years. 
 Manage Models provides full configuration control over all eight model variants across the four core model types — Churn, CLV, Propensity to Buy, and TCLV — for both Profiles and Groups. This goes significantly deeper than the standard Predictive Indicators module, giving users the ability to configure model run parameters, review previous runs, and tune models to specific business contexts. 
 The Bigger Picture: Intelligence Across the Full Contact-to-Lead Journey 
 What makes this stack meaningful is how the capabilities connect. SAP Engagement Cloud ensures the right message is crafted, optimized, delivered at the right time, and personalized to individual behavior. SAP Customer Data Platform ensures the right contacts are targeted in the first place — with predictive scores that surface who is ready to buy, who is at risk of churning, and where lifetime value is concentrated. 
 Together, they shift marketing from a volume game to a precision one. Less guesswork, more signal. Less broadcast, more relevance. And the more data these systems accumulate, the sharper the intelligence becomes — creating a compounding advantage that improves with every campaign, every click, and every conversion. 
 Capabilities covered: Subject Line Generator, Preheader Generator, AI-Assisted Report Builder, Send Time Optimization, Predict, Predictive Indicators, and AI Workbench — all available within SAP Engagement Cloud and SAP Customer Data Platform.

title: SAP System-Based Examinations: Are We Testing Competence or Setting Candidates Up to Fail?
author: ChipoMiranda_Mukwaira
text:
I would like to raise a serious concern about the fairness and design of SAP system-based examinations. 
 I recently went through an SAP Fiori Administration assessment. I completed the assignments, undertook the practical exercises, passed the required assessments and spent considerable time preparing and testing my understanding of the system. 
 Despite all this effort, I received a ZERO. 
 What makes this particularly frustrating is that the assessment is supposed to evaluate practical knowledge and the ability to perform tasks within an SAP environment. 
 I understand that examinations must maintain high standards and that candidates must demonstrate competence. I have absolutely no problem with being challenged or tested rigorously. 
 However, I struggle to understand how a candidate who has completed the learning activities, assignments and practical assessments can end up with a zero without meaningful feedback explaining where the assessment went wrong. 
 It raises some important questions: 

 How transparent is the assessment and marking process? 

 Are candidates being assessed on their actual SAP knowledge or on their ability to navigate the examination platform? 

 Is there sufficient consideration for technical limitations within remote examination environments? 

 What mechanisms exist for candidates to challenge results they believe do not accurately reflect their demonstrated competence? 

 Does a score of zero genuinely mean that a candidate demonstrated no knowledge whatsoever? 
 I am not asking for certification to be handed to me. I am asking for an assessment process that is transparent, consistent and capable of fairly measuring what a candidate actually knows. 
 An examination should identify gaps in competence, not leave candidates questioning whether their competence was ever properly assessed in the first place. 
 SAP invests heavily in building skilled professionals. The certification process should reflect the same commitment to quality, fairness and professional standards. 
 I would appreciate hearing from other SAP learners and certified professionals who have experienced similar situations.

title: Joule A2A: From Customer-Managed to SAP-Managed - Options for BTP Code-Based Agents
author: felixbartler
text:
Many customers used the option to connect custom-built pro-code agents on BTP to (Customer-Managed) Joule. Now, with the re-launch of Joule and Joule Studio, there are a few things to consider moving forward. In this blog post I describe the paths forward for custom-built, BTP-based agents in the new landscape of the Business AI platform. 
 For the bigger picture, everything here sits within the frame set by the SAP reference architecture A2A and MCP for AI Agent Interoperability at SAP — that is the authoritative view of how A2A and MCP fit together across SAP and third-party systems, and it is worth reading before diving into the options below. 
 This post is for developers who already run a custom BTP agent (Python, CAP, or otherwise) connected to Joule — and especially for those who followed my earlier series on wiring pro-code agents to the (then customer-managed) Joule via A2A. That series started with Joule A2A: Connect Code-Based Agents into Joule and built up through authentication with IAS, multi-turn conversations, async communications to principal propagation into S/4HANA. 
 Note: This is the state of November 2026 

 So what changed? 
 CMJ to SMJ 
 At the core, the most significant change is the evolution from Joule 1.0 — what is called Customer-Managed Joule (CMJ) — to Joule Work , which can be considered a 2.0 version and is now "SAP-managed" (SMJ). 
 This managed approach means a few things. In the past, Joule mainly surfaced as a BTP service. You subscribed to it, set up formations and destinations in your subaccounts to connect it to systems, and had to integrate it with other components like Joule Studio, Work Zone, or Document Grounding. 
 A key change now is that Joule Work is not really a BTP service anymore. The way Joule surfaces to customers is via a provisioning flow in SAP for Me — and with it come a number of changes. Since the provisioning flow in SAP for Me now does a lot of the integration and setup work for you, once a solution is provisioned a bunch of tenants are spun up in the background and the system connections are there out of the box. 
 Changes in extensibility 
 With this new Joule, the extensibility options have been reworked as well. Previously, we had the option to pursue a low-code path in the now-called "classic" Joule Studio — to create skills and agents, both of which were quite constrained. In addition, we had the option to pursue a pro-code-based approach by creating capabilities — essentially YAML-based descriptors of functionality — that also exposed skills or agents. In that pro-code YAML approach, we could register an A2A agent via an agent connector (what this series is about). Skills were hard-wired, deterministic sequences of conditions and API calls. 
 Now, in the new world, Joule Studio 2.0 has been launched. It mainly introduces changes on two axes: 
 The design time is now driven by interacting with a coding agent. 
 The runtime is a Kubernetes-based custom-resource environment that gives us artifact-specific benefits. 
 We create Agents, n8n workflows, and agent extensions in Joule Studio 2.0 (and much more coming). 
 In our context, the agent is the relevant artifact for now. How does it look in practice: The coding agent creates a set of Python files to build an A2A-capable agent based on a very familiar LangChain pattern. These agents use MCP tools via an out-of-the-box system connectivity path supporting principal propagation. The managed agent runtime — in which the Python code is deployed — handles authentication out of the box, and the integration into Joule is taken care of via registration through the agent gateway and IAS. Once deployed and the roles are assigned to users, the agents are consumable via Joule. 
 If you built along with the series, this matters: the IAS setup and the principal-propagation chain are now handled by the runtime. The work you put into wiring IAS trust and SAML bearer flows is exactly what you no longer need to do here. But at the same time this also comes with some restraints: Currently in Joule Studio 2.0 this automatic integration towards the APIs does not work for all kinds of APIs. For example take an API that does not support principal propagation. In the past that meant you implemented your own way of guarding that access for your app - in Joule Studio, only APIs where the principal propagation can be enforced from the beginning are accessible. 
 Where does my existing agent go? 
 There are essentially three paths forward for existing BTP agent developments. Here is the quick decision overview before we go into detail: 
 Path Available today? When it fits Main limitation 
 Migrate to Joule Studio 2.0 ✅ Yes New or re-buildable cases; you want PP & auth out of the box Only connects to systems in your SMJ formation (third-party MCP on roadmap) 
 Outbound A2A to Joule Work ⏳ Not yet (roadmap) You want to keep the existing BTP agent as-is Not supported yet; protocol/connection details still to come 
 Joule skills (Markdown) ✅ Yes Simple cases that only need orchestration + connected-system data No custom code; relies on the orchestrator's agentic reasoning 
 Beyond these three, there is a transitional option: you can import existing CMJ capability YAMLs into the new setup. This carries existing investments across short-term but has limited future for new topics — see SAP's Transitioning from Customer-Managed Joule guidance. More on this below. 
 Now let's walk through each of these. 
 Migrate an A2A agent to Joule Studio 
 Here I want to discuss the options and considerations if you are not starting on a green field. Since you already have an agent — maybe written in Python, maybe based on CAP, maybe even in another programming language, and certainly carrying a little complexity — there are a few things to think about. 
 1. Adapt to Joule Studio's connectivity options 
 First and foremost, Joule Studio supports connectivity to the connected systems from your SMJ setup. This means if you connected SMJ to S/4HANA Public Cloud, you can get the coding agent to set you up an MCP server that will talk to the OData APIs available in that system. No need for creating own Destination and Communication Scenarios or API Users. This is super convenient because it comes with principal propagation out of the box. So whenever you have the option, such a managed integration is the way to go and a big leap forward in comparison how we ran extensions in BTP for the past decade! 
 Note: As mentioned above this does come with some restrictions on the API availability - the APIs need to be enabled for Principal Propagation - and for some LoBs like Ariba - that excludes a larger number of them because they were never meant to be used for Agents at the time when they were created many years ago. 
 Integrating with systems not in the SMJ formation 
 More interesting is what is not (yet, as of 9 Nov) possible: connecting any third-party system. If you are pulling data from an on-prem or BW system — which cannot be connected to Joule — then this is a blocker right now. E.g. simple Agents like my Currency Agent using a Third-Party API are affected. 
 Note: There is a roadmap item to support third-party MCP servers that will cover this 
 In Joule Studio, MCP is the protocol to expose data to agents. Maybe you implemented tools in the past based on Python functions that did individual API calls — this is a pattern that will not be that easily possible anymore. 
 This means that right now the described pattern, including the Integration Suite MCP Gateway, is the cleanest way to connect to other data sources after all — because it can translate OData nicely into MCP, and we can then register that with the new agent. The topic of Cloud Connector is also something we would then handle at that point, in the Integration Suite subaccount. 
 You can use MCP Gateway already today in full form - checkout my other post on that. 
 2. Change in Discovery and Registration of Agents 
 The YAML markup model we have seen in the CMJ A2A setup is now gone with Joule Studio 2.0. That means Agents are directly hooked up to the Orchestrator and the intermediary deterministic "Joule Function" logic does not exist anymore. A fixed set of fields are passed to the A2A Agent at runtime - so multi-turn handling etc. are there out of the box. In the past we took care of that ourselves. 
 But with the going away of the YAMLs, also a large part of flexibility in scripting UI elements is now gone. 
 3. Ways of interacting 
 In the old CMJ world, via the YAMLs, we were able to configure some nice modals — this is not really the standard anymore. Instead, Markdown is the main form of communication. So your agent should adapt to Markdown as the communication default. Message in, message out. The orchestrator will format or parse information from the Agent in subsequent processes. 
 4. Managed Runtime 
 While the old BTP based Agents were usually deployed on Cloud Foundry. With the new Joule Studio the Agent is deployed on a kubernetes based environment that is managed by SAP. While Cloud Foundry gives you a lot of control about the environment, scaling etc. with Joule Studio you are mainly running within the constraints of that custom resource definition. The artefacts are grouped in "Solutions" and you will end up with a deployment descriptor called solution.yaml that can contain multiple dependent assets. For example you might have a project including some MCP Servers and a Custom Agent. 
 Action Items for Migration: 
 Instead of own connectivity paths consider using a Joule Studio built (/translated) MCP server to connect to Systems 
 For any third party connectivity be prepared to use an MCP Server - checkout MCP Gateway as an Option 
 Make sure your agent does not rely on custom modals from YAML and rework in Markdown 
 Adapt to use the Managed Runtime from BAIP - that means no own Destination and Auth out of the box + adapt deployment descriptor to asset.yaml 
 Maintain the Agent Card properly - this is now really used for routing from the orchestration 
 Think of the Agent Identity as a new concept to IAM with Agents 
 For a concrete example on the approach I will consider writing another detailed blog. In short: The best approach right now is to use the Pro-Code Flow from Joule Studio via the jl command line. This gives you enough flexibility to start with an existing project structure and then have a coding agent guide you along the way to adapting to the new structure. 
 Connect an agent via A2A to Joule Work 
 The second obvious choice would be to again use A2A — keep the BTP agent as is — and try hooking it up to Joule Work. This is the path that preserves the most of your existing series investment. This is something we call outbound A2A , and it is currently not yet supported and part of a future roadmap. Here, most likely, the way of connecting will not involve the YAML madness anymore. 
 For this topic I will follow up with another post once it is possible. 
 A third way: Joule skills 
 With Joule Work - also the new Agentic Thinking orchestration mode has been announced. It is much more versatile and can be extended with Skills: Markdown-based prompts in combination with scripts that can infuse intelligence and know-how into the main orchestration agent's agentic thinking. Users can select these skills at runtime, and with them you can help the orchestrator perform tasks, given its out-of-the-box ability to retrieve data from the connected systems. Though be aware of the restrictions. While Skills in Joule Work Desktop can even install full-on python packages, the environment in the web has some limitations. Also regarding connecting to arbitrary systems from a skill using curl for example. 
 But anyhow - So many super-simple use cases that in the past were an agent use case might have shifted — with the new possibilities of agentic thinking. So definitely give this one a try. 
 Choose an Approach 
 To conclude: the

title: How to Display Styled Notifications from a Mashup in SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2
author: AlinaPodolski
text:
If you've ever built a mashup for SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2 or SAP Enterprise Service Management, you've probably encountered the same challenge: your embedded web application runs inside an iframe, isolated from the host UI. While you can build your own interface, displaying notifications directly within the SAP application was not possible. Until now. 
 With the new Mashup Initiated Notification feature, external web applications can trigger native SAP notifications using the browser's postMessage API. This allows mashups to display success messages, warnings, errors, and informational messages directly within the SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 interface. 
 In this blog post, I'll demonstrate this functionality using a simple mashup application and explain how you can implement it yourself. 
 See It in Action 
 To demonstrate the feature, I created a small web application and embedded it as a mashup within an Account in SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2. The application allows users to trigger different notification scenarios and inspect the corresponding JSON payloads sent to the host application. 
 Let's start with a simple example. 
 Simple Notifications 
 The first section of the demo application provides four buttons, one for each supported severity level: SUCCESS , INFO , WARNING , and ERROR . Clicking one of these buttons sends a message to the host application, which then displays the corresponding notification using the native SAP UI. 
 Screenshot 1: Simple success notification triggered from the mashup 

 In this example, clicking the Success button triggers the message "Record saved successfully." at the top of the SAP application. The notification appears outside the embedded mashup and uses the standard SAP styling, including the appropriate severity color and icon. The application also displays the JSON payload in the Last Sent Payload section, allowing us to inspect the message sent to the host. 
 Notifications with Multiple Detail Messages 
 In addition to simple notifications, the feature supports more complex scenarios where multiple messages can be grouped into a single notification. 
 The second section of the demo application demonstrates this using two predefined scenarios: Validation Result (mixed) and Order Failed (with details) . For example, clicking Validation Result (mixed) triggers a notification containing several validation results with different severity levels. 
 Screenshot 2: Expanded notification showing multiple validation results 

 As shown above, SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 displays the individual messages with their corresponding severity icons. The notification initially appears in a compact view and can be expanded to reveal all detail messages. This is particularly useful for scenarios where a mashup performs custom validations or interacts with external services that return multiple results. 
 Just like with simple notifications, the demo application displays the complete JSON payload in the Last Sent Payload section. 
 How to Implement It 
 Now that we've seen what the feature looks like, let's take a look at how it works. 
 The integration uses the browser's built-in window.parent.postMessage API to communicate between the embedded mashup and the SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 host application. To trigger a notification, the mashup sends a structured message containing the showMessage operation and the notification parameters. 
 The following JavaScript example demonstrates how to send a notification with multiple detail messages: 
 window.parent.postMessage({
 operation: "showMessage",
 params: {
 message: "Validation completed with issues.",
 severity: "WARNING",
 details: [
 {
 message: "Phone number format is invalid.",
 severity: "ERROR"
 },
 {
 message: "Email address could not be verified.",
 severity: "WARNING"
 },
 {
 message: "Company name was auto-corrected.",
 severity: "INFO"
 },
 {
 message: "Primary contact was set successfully.",
 severity: "SUCCESS"
 }
 ]
 }
}, "*"); 
 The message consists of the following elements: 

 operation: Defines the action to be executed by the host application. For notifications, this must be showMessage . 

 params.message: Contains the primary notification text. 

 params.severity: Defines the severity of the primary notification. 

 params.details: An optional array of additional messages, each with its own severity. 
 The supported severity values are SUCCESS , INFO , WARNING , and ERROR . These values are case sensitive and must be uppercase. For simple notifications, the details array can be omitted. Only the primary message and severity are required. Once the message is sent, the host application handles the notification rendering. No additional UI components or libraries are required within the mashup. 
 Conclusion 
 The Mashup Initiated Notification feature provides a simple way to display native notifications directly within SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 from embedded web applications. Whether you're displaying a simple success message or multiple validation results, the integration requires only a structured JSON payload and a single postMessage call. 
 This makes it easier to provide a consistent user experience without having to implement custom notification components inside your mashups.

title: Replicating Bank Account Numbers Beyond 18 Characters in SAP S/4HANA Using IT0009
author: Sakthi_Soundarya
text:
During the Bank Transfer file generation for Algeria, we encountered an issue where the complete bank account number was not displayed in the report. 
 The bank account number maintained in SuccessFactors Employee Central contained 20 characters. However, only the first 18 characters were replicated to SAP S/4HANA. 
 Initially, we suspected an issue with the report. However, further analysis revealed that the limitation was with the standard Bank Account field in Infotype 0009 (IT0009). 
 This blog explains why the bank account number was truncated during replication and how I resolved it by utilizing the standard Reference Details field (BKREF) in IT0009. 
 Analysis 
 The standard Bank Account field (BANKN) in IT0009 supports a maximum of 18 characters. 
 Since the bank account number maintained in Employee Central contained 20 characters, only the first 18 characters were replicated to the BANKN field in S/4HANA. The remaining two characters were not captured. 
 To overcome this limitation, my initial approach was to create a custom field in IT0009 and replicate the remaining characters into it. 
 However, this would require additional changes wherever the complete bank account number was needed, as the values from the standard and custom fields would have to be combined. 
 Instead, I explored the possibility of using the existing Reference Details field (BKREF) in IT0009. 
 The approach was to replicate the first 18 characters to BANKN and the remaining two characters to BKREF. This would allow us to retain the standard Bank Account field while accommodating the complete 20-character account number. 
 Solution 
 To enable the Reference Details field and configure the replication from Employee Central to S/4HANA, I followed the steps below. I refered to 
 For enabling the BKREF field, I referred to the following SAP Note: SAP Note 2030582 
 Go to transaction SM30 and maintain the relevant configuration in view V_T005 . 

 2. Navigate to view V_T521A and search for the entry DZ . 

 Since the required entry was not available, a new entry had to be created. 

 After completing the configuration, the Reference Details field became available in IT0009 

 3. Now that the Reference Details field is available, the next step is to configure the field mapping for replicating the bank account number from Employee Central to S/4HANA. 
 Navigate to: 
 SPRO → Personnel Management → Integration with SuccessFactors Employee Central → Business Integration Builder → Data Replication from Employee Central → Employee Data → Field Mapping for Employee Data Replication from Employee Central → Define Field Mapping for Employee Data. 
 Select the Payment Information Primary mapping template. 

 4. Create a new field mapping entry to map the remaining two characters of the bank account number to the BKREF field. For this, I used the Pay Sequence EC field as the source field, since its value was maintained in Employee Central but was not replicated to S/4HANA. 

 5. Configure Generic Value Conversion 
 For configuring the required string manipulation, I referred to SAP Note 3275329 . 
 The Generic Value Conversion rule requires a source EC field to have a value to execute the conversion. Therefore, I used the Pay Sequence field as the source field for the mapping. 
 The objective was to prepend the original bank account number to this field and then extract the last two characters for replication to BKREF. 

 6. Once the field mapping and conversion rules are maintained, trigger Employee Data Replication from Employee Central to S/4HANA 

 The replication was successful, and the remaining two characters were populated in the BKREF field. 
 Conclusion 
 By utilizing the standard Reference Details field (BKREF) in IT0009, we were able to overcome the 18-character limitation of the standard Bank Account field (BANKN). 
 This approach helped us accommodate the complete 20-character bank account number without introducing an additional custom field. 
 The complete bank account number can now be obtained by concatenating BANKN and BKREF, wherever required, including payslips and other reports.

title: Beyond FOR ALL ENTRIES: Are you still using it on S/4HANA, or have CTEs & Joins taken over?
author: Gayathri_S
text:
Hi SAP Community, 
 During a recent code review for an S/4HANA migration project, our team had a healthy debate over an age-old habit: FOR ALL ENTRIES (FAE) . 
 For decades in ECC / NetWeaver, FAE was the gold standard to avoid nested selects and bypass heavy joins on legacy row-store databases. But on SAP HANA, with in-memory columnar storage and modern ABAP SQL (7.40+ / 7.50+), the trade-offs look very different. 
 1. The Classic Habit We Still See Everywhere 
 " Step 1: Mandatory check to prevent catastrophic full-table scan
IF lt_vbak IS NOT INITIAL.

 " Step 2: Sorting and deleting duplicates to optimize driver table
 SORT lt_vbak BY vbeln.
 DELETE ADJACENT DUPLICATES FROM lt_vbak COMPARING vbeln.

 " Step 3: FAE query
 SELECT vbeln, posnr, matnr, netwr
 FROM vbap
 FOR ALL ENTRIES IN @lt_vbak
 WHERE vbeln = @lt_vbak-vbeln
 INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_vbap).

ENDIF. 
 The Pain Points: 
 The Empty Driver Table Trap: If lt_vbak is accidentally initial, SAP ignores the WHERE clause and executes an unrestricted SELECT * across the entire database table. 
 Implicit DISTINCT Overhead: FAE silently eliminates duplicate result rows across the selected fields, adding sorting overhead on the database execution plan. 
 Array Splitting & Network Overhead: NetWeaver chunks large internal tables into batches (usually 5,000–10,000 records), requiring multiple network roundtrips to the HANA database. 
 2. The Modern Alternative: Common Table Expressions (CTE) & Joins 
 With modern ABAP SQL, we can push down the entire operation into a single roundtrip using Common Table Expressions ( WITH 😞 
 " Single DB roundtrip with Common Table Expression (CTE)
WITH +open_orders AS (
 SELECT vbeln, erdat, vkorg
 FROM vbak
 WHERE vkorg = @lv_sales_org
 AND erdat >= @lv_from_date
)
SELECT o~vbeln, o~vkorg, i~posnr, i~matnr, i~netwr
 FROM +open_orders AS o
 INNER JOIN vbap AS i
 ON o~vbeln = i~vbeln
 INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_order_details). 
 Even when your driver data originates from application logic inside an internal table, modern ABAP (7.52+) allows using the internal table directly as a SQL data source : 
 IF lt_vbak IS NOT INITIAL.
 SELECT i~vbeln, i~posnr, i~matnr, i~netwr
 FROM @lt_vbak AS o
 INNER JOIN vbap AS i
 ON o~vbeln = i~vbeln
 INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_items).
ENDIF. 
 Where It Gets Tricky in Practice 
 HANA Memory Footprint: Passing very large internal tables (e.g. 100k+ rows) directly into Open SQL can occasionally cause temporary memory spikes on the DB layer. 
 ABAP Cloud & Clean ABAP: In Tier-1 development, direct SQL on standard tables is replaced by released CDS Views and APIs, making classical FAE patterns completely obsolete. 
 Let's Discuss: 
 Has your team officially banned FOR ALL ENTRIES in your coding guidelines, or is it still allowed in specific edge cases? 
 Have you observed any real-world production cases where FAE actually performed better than an inner join or CTE on HANA? 
 How is your team handling developer enablement to move away from procedural table loops toward SQL Pushdown and CDS Views? 
 Looking forward to hearing thoughts and experiences from other SAP architects and developers!

title: Auto-populating Project Definition Dates to Level-1 CAPEX WBS in CJ20N
author: Gayathri_S
text:
Hi SAP Community, 
 I am working on a requirement in SAP PS (CJ20N) where the Basic Start Date ( PLFAZ ) and Basic Finish Date ( PLSEZ ) entered at the Project Definition header need to be automatically copied to the Level-1 CAPEX WBS element when saving the project. 
 Business Logic: 
 Special Projects ( RFTA , CHTA 😞 Only one Level-1 WBS exists, so it directly inherits the Project Definition dates. 
 Standard Projects ( RFPA , RFCA , CHPA , etc.): Needs to identify if the Level-1 WBS is CAPEX (checking 'C' at character 10 / token 3 of the coding mask) before assigning the dates. 
 The Technical Challenge: 
 Table PRTE : When a WBS is newly created, standard SAP does not insert a record into table PRTE . A record only exists in PRTE if a user manually visits the "Dates" tab in CJ20N and enters dates. 
 Standard BAPIs: Calling BAPI_BUS2054_CHANGE_MULTI or BAPI_PROJECT_MAINTAIN synchronously inside a save BAdI fails because CJ20N holds active ENQUEUE locks on the project. 
 BAdI Selection: In WORKBREAKDOWN_UPDATE~AT_SAVE , the IT_WBS_ELEMENT table is empty if only Project Definition header dates are updated. Therefore, BAdI PROJECTDEF_UPDATE~AT_SAVE was chosen since it directly provides IM_PROJECTDEFINITION-PLFAZ and PLSEZ . 
 Proposed Solution: 
 Inside BAdI IF_EX_PROJECTDEF_UPDATE~AT_SAVE : 
 Read PLFAZ and PLSEZ from IM_PROJECTDEFINITION . 
 Fetch Level-1 WBS elements from PRPS where psphi = im_projectdefinition-pspnr AND stufe = 1 . 
 Check the project coding mask for CAPEX qualification. 
 Attempt an UPDATE on table PRTE ( PSTRT , PENDE , PDAUR , PEINH = 'TAG' , FLGVM = 'X' ). 
 If sy-subrc <> 0 (record does not exist yet), execute a direct INSERT into PRTE with the initial scheduling fields. 
 Discussion Question: 
 While direct UPDATE / INSERT into PRTE with FLGVM = 'X' runs seamlessly within the same CJ20N save LUW and avoids lock issues, direct standard table inserts are usually discouraged in SAP. 
 Has anyone implemented a direct INSERT into PRTE within a BAdI in production? Have you seen any negative side-effects on basic scheduling or downstream CJ20N functions? 
 Or is it strictly recommended to push this to an asynchronous background RFC calling BAPI_BUS2054_CHANGE_MULTI to let standard SAP create the PRTE entry? 
 Would appreciate your inputs and recommended best practices! 
 Thanks in advance!

title: How SAP Store Certification Turns into Customer Trust for Vertex
author: Andreia Bessa
text:
Tax is one of those business functions nobody wants to think about until something goes wrong. Vertex, one of the largest indirect tax software companies in the world, has spent more than two decades making sure that for SAP customers, nothing does. 

 According to Vertex’s Ken Crovetti and Scott Druckenmiller, the trust that makes that possible doesn’t come only from the product. It comes from being certified and visible on SAP Store . 

 Why “disjointed” is the enemy 

 Druckenmiller, SAP partner channel sales manager at Vertex, describes the problem the partnership is built to solve: companies buying a stack of point solutions that don’t talk to each other. “Nobody wants to buy a point solution anymore,” Druckenmiller says. “Everybody wants to make sure all the dots connect.” 
 Discover, try, and buy solutions from SAP and partners 

 Explore SAP Store 

 Vertex’s answer is to embed itself so deeply into SAP’s order-to-cash and procure-to-pay processes that the two systems function as one. Every order that runs through SAP triggers a tax calculation from Vertex at the same moment pricing is calculated, tied to the same master data—customers, products, vendors—that SAP already manages. Break that connection and orders stall. Keep it intact and you get what SAP calls a “no-touch order,” one that moves from creation to invoice to the general ledger without anyone stepping in. 

 Crovetti, business development lead for the SAP relationship at Vertex, frames the value in terms customers immediately understand: cash flow. Miscalculate tax, set aside too much or too little, and a company’s cash position takes the hit. “We want to keep that cash flow with you,” Crovetti says, “so you can grow, get bigger, better, faster, more efficient.” 

 Certification as the trust signal 

 Crovetti works directly between Vertex’s sales organization and SAP’s—his job is to be a trusted advisor to joint customers. SAP Store is central to how he does that. 

 Druckenmiller frames the online marketplace as a filter for customers that are otherwise bombarded by vendors claiming SAP compatibility: “[SAP] Store is a great way for them to understand which ones are SAP blessed—and not just blessed, certified.” That certification is what separates a claim from a guarantee. 

 Crovetti uses the word “matchmakers” to describe what SAP Store enables: connecting Vertex, SAP account teams, the customer, and sometimes a systems integrator around a shared need, before a formal sales process even begins. “[SAP] Store becomes that window to connect everybody,” he says. 

 Druckenmiller makes the prospect experience concrete with a simple analogy: “It’s no different than how we go online and look at buying a car. You know everything about your car before you walk into the dealership. We want to give our customers that same experience.” To that end, Vertex puts short demo videos on SAP Store—showing the tax engine running inside the SAP interface, not Vertex’s own UI—so a prospect can see what it looks like before committing to a full discovery cycle. 

 Part of the family 

 Crovetti puts it plainly: once you’ve gone through SAP’s certification process and landed on SAP Store , “You’re part of the family.” That’s not just symbolic. It means SAP’s credibility transfers to partners who’ve earned it—and that the trust Vertex would otherwise have to build from scratch with every new prospect is already there when the conversation starts. 

 “[SAP] Store becomes not just a marketplace,” Druckenmiller says, “but an opportunity for customers to find certified solutions that can fill a gap”—whether that’s cloud ERP transformation, a compliance need, or something in between.
